name: How Learning Works
author: Recurse
subject: humanities
description: The research behind Recurse: forgetting, spacing, retrieval, interleaving, pretesting, self-explanation, dual coding and study myths.

lesson.intro: Most people study in ways that feel productive but fade fast. Cognitive science has found better methods, which explain why Recurse asks before it shows and spaces your reviews. Learn how memories fade, what makes them last, and which habits do not hold up.
objectives: Explain the forgetting curve and why spaced reviews and sleep make memories last
Use retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving in your own study
Explain how pretesting, self-explanation, dual coding and worked examples help
Spot study habits that feel productive but are not, including learning styles
Connect each part of Recurse to the research behind it

sections.title: Forgetting, consolidation and sleep
sections.key: Forgetting is fastest in the first hours and days, then slows; each well-timed review flattens the curve, and sleep consolidates what you learned.
sections.body:
In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann **Ebbinghaus** memorized nonsense syllables such as DAX and BOK, so he could not lean on anything he already knew. Then he measured how fast he relearned them after delays from 20 minutes to a month. His results, published in 1885 and replicated many times since, form the **forgetting curve**.

[[visual]]

Meaningful material fades more slowly than nonsense, but the shape is the same. Two more findings matter:

- **Relearning is faster** than first learning: even when you cannot recall something, a trace remains.
- **Each well-timed review flattens the curve**, so the next drop takes longer.

Memories keep changing after you study. **Consolidation** stabilizes a new memory over the following hours and days, much of it during sleep, when the brain replays recent experiences. Losing sleep weakens consolidation and makes new memories harder to form the next day.

visual.title: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve
visual.caption: Share of the original learning time he saved when relearning after each delay. The big drop comes first, then the loss slows.

sections.tip: Study in the evening and then sleep well. An all-nighter before an exam costs the consolidation that would have kept what you studied.
sections.pitfall: Treating forgetting as failure. Some forgetting is normal and even useful: reviewing just as a memory starts to fade is what makes it stronger.

check.question: Ebbinghaus found that relearning a list he could no longer recall took less time than learning it the first time. What does this show?
choices: He had simply become a faster reader of nonsense syllables
Short nonsense syllables are always easier the second time
A trace of the list remained even though he could not recall it
Forgetting had not yet started when he relearned the list
check.explanation: Ebbinghaus called this "savings". A memory you cannot retrieve can still leave a trace, which is why reviewing forgotten material is faster than learning it from scratch.

sections.title: Spacing and retrieval practice
sections.key: Spread reviews out over time and recall answers from memory instead of rereading: the same study time then lasts far longer.
sections.body:
**Spaced repetition** puts the forgetting curve to work: review several times with gaps in between, instead of **massed practice** (cramming) in one sitting. For the same total time, spacing gives much better long-term retention. Cramming can get you through tomorrow's test, then fades.

The best gap grows with how long you need to remember: a day suits a test next week, but knowledge for next year needs gaps of weeks or months. A 2006 meta-analysis by Cepeda and colleagues, pooling hundreds of experiments, confirmed it.

**Retrieval practice** means pulling information out of memory: answering questions, flashcards, writing what you remember on a blank page. Recall strengthens a memory more than seeing the answer again, the **testing effect**, and shows honestly what you know.

[[visual]]

Recurse combines both:

[[visual 2]]

items.title: Reread the passage
points: Slightly better on a test 5 minutes later

items.title: Practiced recalling it
points: Remembered much more a week later

steps.label: It asks before it shows the answer
The FSRS scheduler estimates your chance of recall
The card returns when that chance falls to your target
Each success makes the memory more durable
steps.detail: So the gaps grow from days to weeks to months

sections.pitfall: Reviewing too soon. Going over something you saw a minute ago feels easy and teaches little; a gap long enough that recall takes effort is what builds durable memory.

check.question: Which of these is a form of retrieval practice?
choices: Reading through your notes again slowly and carefully
Covering your notes and writing down what you remember
Highlighting the most important sentences in a chapter
Listening to a recording of the lecture a second time
check.explanation: Retrieval practice means producing information from memory. Writing what you remember from a blank page counts; rereading, highlighting and relistening only expose you to the material again.

sections.title: Desirable difficulties: interleaving and elaboration
sections.key: Desirable difficulties such as interleaving and elaboration make practice feel harder but build learning that lasts, so how practice feels is a poor guide.
sections.body:
Robert Bjork coined **desirable difficulties** for conditions that make learning feel slower and harder now but improve long-term retention; spacing and retrieval are two. The key idea: **performance** during practice is not **learning**. Smooth, easy practice feels like progress while building little that lasts.

**Interleaving** mixes problem types in one session instead of blocking them:

[[visual]]

**Elaboration** connects new material to what you know: asking how and why, comparing ideas, inventing your own examples. The **Feynman technique**, named after the physicist Richard Feynman, is a popular way to do it:

[[visual 2]]

A difficulty is desirable only if effort can overcome it. Material far beyond your current knowledge just frustrates; step back to simpler material first.

visual.title: Rohrer and Taylor (2007), a math study

items.title: Blocked
items.sub: A A A B B B
points: You know the method before reading each problem
20% on a test a week later

items.title: Interleaved
items.sub: A C B A B C
points: You must decide which method fits, as a real test demands
63% on a test a week later

visual.caption: Interleaving helps most when the categories are similar and easy to confuse.

visual.title: The Feynman technique

steps.label: Pick a concept and explain it in plain words, as if to a beginner
Notice where your explanation gets vague or stalls
Go back to the source to fill that gap

visual.loop: Repeat until it is simple and complete

sections.deeper:
**Interleaving is not magic everywhere.** A 2019 meta-analysis by Brunmair and Richter found a moderate benefit overall. It was strongest for telling apart similar categories, such as paintings by different artists, and absent or even reversed for some materials, such as lists of vocabulary words.

**Why blocked practice fools you.** When every problem in a set uses the same method, you never practice the hardest part of a real exam: recognizing which method a problem needs.
sections.pitfall: Judging a method by how easy practice feels. Smooth, comfortable practice often means little is being learned, while effortful practice usually means more is.

check.question: Which study habit is an example of elaboration?
choices: Copying each definition out word for word into a notebook
Reading the whole chapter a second time before the test
Highlighting every key sentence in the chapter in yellow
Asking why a fact is true and linking it to something you know
check.explanation: Elaboration connects new material to existing knowledge by asking how and why and by generating examples. Copying, rereading and highlighting keep you on the surface of the text.

sections.title: Pretesting and self-explanation: try first, then explain
sections.key: Trying to answer before you are taught, then studying the feedback, makes the answer stick; explaining steps to yourself or teaching them deepens understanding.
sections.body:
Before a lesson on volcanoes, try to answer: why do most volcanoes sit near the edges of tectonic plates? You will probably get it wrong or half right. Strangely, that failed attempt makes the explanation that follows stick better than simply reading it would.

This is the **pretesting effect**: a wrong guess exposes what you do not know and focuses your attention when the answer arrives. The feedback is essential; guessing without ever seeing the answer does not help.

[[visual]]

**Self-explanation** turns reading into thinking: after each step of an example, ask why it follows and how it connects to what you already know.

visual.title: Try first, then explain
rows: Answer before you are taught, then study the answer
Kornell, Hays and Bjork (2009): guessers remembered more, though their guesses were almost always wrong
Wrestle with a problem before being taught the method
Sinha and Kapur (2021): helps conceptual understanding when the struggle is well designed and followed by solid instruction
Chi and colleagues (1994): beat reading the text twice
Fiorella and Mayer (2013): teaching on video beat studying for a test, a week later

sections.pitfall: Skipping the feedback. A pretest or a struggle helps only when you study the correct answer afterward; guessing on its own teaches nothing.

check.question: In pretesting studies, why does answering before studying help even when the answer is wrong?
choices: Wrong answers fade so fast that they leave no trace at all
It only helps when the guess happens to be correct
The failed attempt primes attention, so the correct answer sticks better when it is shown
It works only because it takes longer than reading
check.explanation: A retrieval attempt, even a failed one, exposes the gap and prepares you to encode the answer. The studies compared equal study time, so the extra time is not the explanation, and guesses were usually wrong.

sections.title: Working memory and cognitive load
sections.key: Working memory holds only about four new chunks for a few seconds, so cut clutter, break topics into steps, and start beginners on worked examples.
sections.body:
**Working memory** is the mental workspace for what you are thinking about right now, like a phone number you are about to dial. It is small and brief: about four chunks of new information (an older estimate was seven, plus or minus two), fading within seconds without rehearsal. **Long-term memory** has no practical limit.

A **chunk** is a meaningful unit. The digits 1, 9, 8, 9 are four items to a young child but one chunk, a year, to someone who knows history. Through **chunking**, experts build large, organized units that let them handle more at once in their field.

[[visual]]

**Worked examples** help beginners because they show each step without forcing a search for a method (Sweller and Cooper, 1985). As skill grows, fade the help:

[[visual 2]]

Too much guidance for someone who already knows the method backfires: the **expertise reversal effect**.

visual.title: Cognitive load theory (John Sweller)
rows: The material itself: how many elements must be held together. It depends on what you already know
How it is presented: cluttered slides, text split from the diagram it explains, notifications
The effort spent actually building understanding
visual.caption: Good design cuts extraneous load and breaks complex topics into smaller steps.

steps.label: One with the last step missing

sections.pitfall: Packing slides or notes with decoration. Every extra element competes for working memory; cut anything that does not help the explanation.

check.question: Who tends to benefit most from studying worked examples?
choices: Beginners, because examples cut the load of searching for a method
Experts, because they can skim the examples quickly and move on
Everyone equally, whatever their level of skill or experience
No one, because examples replace the real thinking learners need
check.explanation: For novices, a worked example shows each step without the heavy load of searching for a method. As skill grows the benefit shrinks, and solving problems yourself becomes more useful.

sections.title: Dual coding, and how Recurse puts it together
sections.key: Words plus meaningful pictures give two linked routes back to a memory, and that helps everyone; decorative images only add load.
sections.body:
Read "the left ventricle pumps blood out to the body" and you have one route back to that fact. Read it beside a labeled diagram of the heart and you have two. Allan Paivio's **dual coding** theory (1986) says words and images are handled by partly separate systems, so material stored both ways has more routes back.

Richard Mayer (2009) made it practical: words plus relevant pictures beat words alone, especially with each label right on the part it describes.

Two cautions. The picture must carry meaning: a decorative stock photo adds load and can distract. And dual coding is for **everyone**: the benefit comes from two linked representations, not from matching "visual learners".

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Every learning mode keeps what research supports for everyone: retrieval, spacing, interleaving and feedback.

The FSRS scheduler times each review just before you would forget

sections.pitfall: Adding pictures for decoration. Only images that explain the idea help; decorative ones compete for attention and can make learning worse.

check.question: Which is the best example of dual coding?
choices: A page of text beside an unrelated photo of a smiling student
Reading the same paragraph aloud twice
Highlighting key words in three different colors
A labeled diagram of the heart, each label placed on the part it names
check.explanation: Dual coding pairs words with a meaningful image of the same idea, here labels sitting on the structures they name. A decorative photo carries no meaning, and repetition or color-coding stays within one channel.

sections.title: Myths: learning styles, rereading and highlighting
sections.key: Matching teaching to learning styles, rereading and highlighting feel helpful but do little; test yourself from memory, spread out over time.
sections.body:
Some of the most popular beliefs about studying do not hold up.

[[visual]]

A large 2013 review by Dunlosky and colleagues rated ten common techniques:

[[visual 2]]

A quick test for any study method: does it make you produce answers from memory, spread out over time? If not, it is probably weaker than it feels. To check whether you really know a chapter, close the book and answer questions about it from memory.

That is why Recurse does not assign you a learning style. Its preference quiz suggests a mode you will enjoy and stick with, and its recall experiment measures what actually helped you: study invented words by rereading, self-testing or picturing them, then get tested on all of them.

visual.title: Three popular myths
rows: **Learning styles**: teach visual, auditory or kinesthetic learners their own way

People have preferences, but Pashler and colleagues (2008) found almost no well-designed evidence that matching helps. Match the format to the content (a map for geography, audio for pronunciation) and combine words with pictures for everyone
Familiar text feels easy to process, and that fluency is mistaken for knowing it: an **illusion of competence**. Recognizing a page is far easier than recalling it
It is passive, and draws attention to isolated phrases instead of how ideas connect

visual.title: Dunlosky et al. (2013)
rows: Interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation (asking why), self-explanation

sections.pitfall: Using "I'm a visual learner" as a reason to skip retrieval. Whatever your preferences, recalling answers and spacing your reviews still do the heavy lifting.

check.question: A large 2013 review of study techniques rated which of these as highly useful?
choices: Highlighting text
Practice testing
Rereading notes
Summarizing text
check.explanation: Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing and distributed practice as high utility. Highlighting, rereading and summarizing were all rated low utility.

keyTerms.definition: The pattern in which memory drops quickly soon after learning and then more slowly, unless it is reviewed.
The process, much of it during sleep, that stabilizes a new memory and integrates it into long-term storage.
Reviewing material several times with growing gaps between reviews instead of all at once.
The finding that retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than restudying it.
Mixing different types of problems or topics within one practice session.
A challenge during learning, such as spacing or testing, that slows practice but improves long-term retention.
The small, short-lived mental workspace that holds what you are thinking about right now.
The demand a task places on working memory.
The finding that attempting to answer questions before studying, even wrongly, improves later learning once the answers are shown.
Explaining to yourself why each step or idea holds and how it connects to what you know, while you study.
Learning material through both words and meaningful images, giving two linked routes back to the memory.

summary: Forgetting is fastest right after learning; each well-timed review flattens the curve.
Spaced reviews and recalling answers from memory beat cramming and rereading.
Interleaving and elaboration feel harder but build learning that lasts and transfers.
Try before you are taught, explain in your own words, and pair words with meaningful pictures.
Working memory holds a few chunks: cut clutter and start beginners on worked examples.
Sleep consolidates memories; learning styles, rereading and highlighting are weaker than they feel.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why answering a flashcard from memory a few days from now will help them more than rereading their notes three times tonight.

questions.question: What did Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve show?
choices: Memories fade at a steady rate, losing the same amount each day
Forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows down
Forgetting begins only about a week after learning
Material learned once is kept for life if it was understood
questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus lost much of each list within the first day, after which the rate of loss slowed. A steady rate is the common misreading. Meaningful material fades more slowly than nonsense syllables, but it still fades without review.

questions.question: Which German psychologist first measured the forgetting curve, publishing his results in 1885?
questions.explanation: Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and measured how much faster he could relearn them after different delays. His curve has been replicated many times since.

questions.question: A student plans to stay up all night reviewing before an exam. Based on sleep research, what is the main problem with this plan?
choices: Sleep plays no part in memory, so the only cost is feeling tired
Memories are stored only while awake, so extra hours awake help
Skipping sleep weakens consolidation and hurts next-day memory and focus
All-night study works as long as the student rereads everything twice
questions.explanation: During sleep, especially deep sleep, the brain stabilizes recently learned material. A night without sleep also leaves attention and the ability to form new memories impaired the next day, so the extra hours are bought at a high price.

questions.question: Two students each spend three hours on a topic. One studies in a single evening; the other does three one-hour sessions spread over a week. Who is likely to remember more a month later?
choices: The single-evening student, because the material was learned in one go
Both about the same, because their total study time was equal
The single-evening student, as long as the session ended with a review
The student who spread the sessions over a week
questions.explanation: This is the spacing effect: with equal total time, spreading study out produces far more durable memory than massing it. Cramming can work for a test the next morning, but the material fades quickly afterward.

questions.question: What is the name for the finding that recalling information from memory strengthens it more than restudying it?
questions.explanation: The testing effect, also called the retrieval practice effect, shows that recall is itself a learning event, not just a check of what you know.

questions.question: In a 2006 study, students either reread a passage or practiced recalling it. Rereading gave slightly better scores on a test five minutes later. What happened on a test one week later?
choices: Both groups scored about the same
The rereading group kept its lead
The recall group remembered substantially more
Both groups had forgotten nearly everything
questions.explanation: After a week, the students who had practiced recall remembered far more, about 56% of the ideas against 42%. Rereading gives a short-term boost and a feeling of fluency, but retrieval builds memory that lasts.

questions.question: Why does a spaced repetition system like Recurse wait longer before showing a card again each time you recall it correctly?
choices: Each correct recall makes the memory more durable, so it fades more slowly
Cards you already know are treated as less important to the course
Longer gaps exist mainly so the app can fit more new cards into each day
A memory stops fading for good once you have recalled it correctly twice
questions.explanation: Each successful retrieval makes a memory more stable, so it takes longer to fall to the point where review is needed. Reviewing near that point gives the most benefit for the least time. Memories never stop fading entirely, which is why reviews continue at longer intervals.

questions.question: Explain why Recurse asks you to answer before it shows the answer, instead of simply showing you the facts to reread.
questions.answer: Pulling an answer out of memory is itself a learning event: effortful retrieval strengthens the memory and makes it easier to retrieve next time. Rereading only feels productive because the material looks familiar, and it gives no honest signal of what you could recall on your own.
questions.explanation: This is the testing effect. Answering first also tells the scheduler how well you know each card, so it can space the next review appropriately.

questions.question: A student preparing for a geometry test can do 10 area problems, then 10 volume problems, then 10 angle problems, or shuffle all 30 together. Which approach does research favor, and why?
choices: Shuffling, because choosing the method for each problem is part of the skill
Blocks, because repeating one method many times builds fluency fastest
Blocks, because mixing several topics at once overloads working memory
Either way, because only the total amount of practice time matters
questions.explanation: Interleaving forces you to decide which method fits each problem, which is what a test demands. In one study it roughly tripled scores a week later, even though practice felt harder and went worse. Blocked practice feels fluent only because you know the method before reading each problem.

questions.question: What term did psychologist Robert Bjork coin for conditions that make learning feel harder but improve long-term retention?
questions.explanation: Desirable difficulties include spacing, retrieval practice and interleaving. They slow apparent progress during practice but produce learning that lasts. A difficulty is desirable only if the learner can overcome it with effort.

questions.question: Which step is at the heart of the Feynman technique?
choices: Copying the textbook's explanation word for word until it sticks
Reading an expert's summary several times before a test
Memorizing key terms with a mnemonic before learning their meaning
Explaining the idea simply, then fixing the parts where it breaks down
questions.explanation: The method is to explain the concept in plain words as if to a beginner, notice where you get vague or stuck, go back to the source and try again. It combines retrieval with elaboration and exposes gaps that rereading hides.

questions.question: Explain the difference between performance during practice and learning, and why it matters when choosing study methods.
questions.answer: Performance is how well you do while practicing; learning is the lasting change that shows up later. Cramming, blocked practice and rereading boost performance in the moment but fade, while spacing, retrieval and interleaving feel slower yet give better long-term results, so how practice feels is a poor guide to what works.
questions.explanation: Bjork's distinction explains why learners often prefer weaker methods: they judge by how fluent practice feels. The real test is what you can do days or weeks later.

questions.question: Why is a long list of unfamiliar terms hard to learn in a single pass?
choices: Long-term memory has limited room and fills up quickly with new words
New words can only be stored during sleep, not while you are reading
Working memory holds only a few new chunks, so new items push out old ones
The brain automatically filters out information it has never seen before
questions.explanation: Working memory can hold only about four chunks of new information at a time. Long-term memory has no practical limit, so the bottleneck is getting items through working memory, which is why small sets and repeated review work better.

questions.question: A diagram is on one slide and its explanation is on the next, so learners must flip back and forth to connect them. What kind of load does this add?
choices: Intrinsic load, because the topic itself is complex and difficult
Extraneous load, because the layout rather than the content creates it
Germane load, because the extra effort deepens your understanding
No extra load at all, because each slide is simple on its own
questions.explanation: Extraneous load comes from how material is presented, not from the material itself. Holding the diagram in mind while reading separate text wastes working memory; putting the explanation on the diagram removes that load.

questions.question: What is the name for grouping separate items into a larger meaningful unit, such as remembering the digits 1, 9, 8, 9 as the year 1989?
questions.explanation: Chunking lets working memory hold more by treating several items as one. Experts handle complex material easily because long-term memory supplies them with large, well-organized chunks.

questions.question: What does research show about teaching people in their preferred "learning style", such as visual, auditory or kinesthetic?
choices: Well-controlled studies find little or no benefit from matching
Matching teaching to a learner's style reliably doubles retention
Only visual learners benefit, because most people think in images
Styles matter a great deal for children but not for adults
questions.explanation: People do have preferences, but a 2008 review by Pashler and colleagues found almost no well-designed evidence that matching instruction to a preferred style improves learning. Matching the format to the content, and combining words with pictures for everyone, works better.

questions.question: Why do rereading and highlighting feel effective even though they produce little lasting learning?
choices: They do strengthen recall, but only when done right before a test
They work well, but only for people who are mainly visual learners
They take so long that students assume they must be learning something
Familiar text feels easy to process, and the ease is mistaken for mastery
questions.explanation: Seeing material again makes it feel fluent and familiar, an illusion of competence, but recognizing text is much easier than recalling it. A large 2013 review rated both rereading and highlighting as low-utility techniques.

questions.question: Match each research-backed strategy to where it shows up in Recurse.

pairs.right: Answering every card before seeing the answer
FSRS scheduling each review just before you would forget
Daily review mixing cards from different topics
A question before each lesson section in Test me first mode
Putting each idea in your own words in Teach it back mode
Interactive diagrams and simulators inside lessons

questions.explanation: Each Recurse feature exists because of a research finding. The modes change the order, but retrieval, spacing and interleaving run underneath all of them.

questions.question: Match each study to its main finding.

pairs.right: Recall beats rereading a week later
Little evidence for matching learning styles

questions.explanation: These five anchor the lesson: forgetting is fast at first, retrieval beats restudy over time, styles-matching lacks evidence, explaining to yourself deepens understanding, and words plus images give memory two routes.

questions.question: What is the name for the finding that trying to answer questions before studying the material improves later learning, even when the guesses are wrong?
questions.explanation: Kornell, Hays and Bjork (2009) showed that unsuccessful retrieval attempts followed by the answer beat spending the same time just studying. Feedback after the attempt is what makes it work.

questions.question: Which statement describes dual coding?
choices: Studying two subjects at the same time to save hours
Teaching people only in their preferred learning style
Pairing words with relevant images gives two linked routes back to a memory
Writing every note out twice
questions.explanation: Paivio's dual coding theory says verbal and visual information are processed partly separately, so storing an idea both ways makes it easier to retrieve. It applies to everyone, unlike the learning-styles idea.

questions.question: A teacher adds diagrams to a lesson "because some students are visual learners." What does the research suggest?
choices: Only the visual learners will benefit, so others can skip the diagrams
Meaningful diagrams help nearly everyone, so keep them, but not because of learning styles
Diagrams overload working memory and should be removed
Diagrams help only when students pick their own colors
questions.explanation: Words plus relevant pictures beat words alone for learners in general (Mayer's multimedia research), while matching instruction to self-described styles shows little benefit (Pashler et al., 2008). Right practice, wrong reason.

questions.question: When is struggling with a problem before being taught the method most likely to help?
choices: When the learner is never shown the correct method
When the problem is far beyond anything the learner could attempt
When the struggle replaces instruction entirely
When solid instruction and feedback follow the struggle
questions.explanation: Productive failure works when the struggle prepares you for an explanation that then arrives. Without instruction afterward, or with a problem you cannot even engage with, the difficulty is no longer desirable.

questions.question: Select every technique that Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) rated as high or moderate utility.
choices: Practice testing
Distributed practice
Interleaved practice
Highlighting
Rereading
Summarization
questions.explanation: Practice testing and distributed practice were rated high utility, and interleaved practice (with elaborative interrogation and self-explanation) moderate. Highlighting, rereading and summarization were rated low utility.

questions.question: Put the steps of the Feynman technique in order.
items: Pick a concept and explain it in plain words, as if to a beginner
Notice where your explanation gets vague or stalls
Go back to the source to fill that gap
questions.explanation: Explaining first is a retrieval attempt that exposes the gaps; the source then fills them, and the second, simpler explanation checks that the gap is really closed.

questions.question: By default, Recurse brings a card back when its predicted chance of recall falls to what percentage?
questions.explanation: The FSRS scheduler aims for 90% retention by default: it predicts when your chance of recalling a card drops to that level and schedules the review then. Each successful recall pushes the next review further out.

questions.question: As a learner gets better at a type of problem, what should happen to worked examples?
choices: Even more detailed examples should be added
The steps should be faded out until the learner solves problems alone
Examples should be replaced by rereading the chapter
Nothing, because examples help experts exactly as much as beginners
questions.explanation: Worked examples help most at the start. Fading the steps hands the work over gradually, and too much guidance for someone who already knows the method backfires (the expertise reversal effect).

questions.question: You need to remember some material for an exam six months away. Which review plan fits the research best?
choices: Review it every day for the next week, then stop
Review it in one long session the night before the exam
Review it with gaps that grow from days to weeks to months
Review it once, a year from now
questions.explanation: The best gap grows with the time you need to retain the material, and expanding gaps keep each review effortful but successful. A week of daily review fades long before the exam, and cramming fades right after it.

questions.question: After rereading a chapter, a student feels confident she knows it. What is the most reliable way to check?
choices: Read it once more to be sure
Notice how familiar the pages look
Highlight the parts she remembers
Close the book and try to answer questions about it from memory
questions.explanation: Familiarity is not recall: recognizing a page is much easier than producing its content. Testing yourself gives an honest signal and strengthens the memory at the same time.
